questions.q: Why does the trigger in this project enqueue a Queueable job instead of making the callout directly?
options: Because triggers cannot reference custom objects
Because triggers cannot query SOQL
Because the trigger's own transaction has pending DML context, and callouts can't run while pending DML exists in the same transaction
Because Queueable Apex is always faster than a direct callout
questions.explain: This directly applies the Lesson 7 transaction-ordering rule — the callout is deferred into a separate Queueable transaction rather than conflicting with the trigger's own pending DML.

questions.q: Inside the OrderSyncJob's execute() method, in what order do the callout and the DML update happen, and why?
options: They must happen in two separate Queueable jobs entirely
The DML and callout happen simultaneously in parallel threads
DML first, then the callout, since order doesn't matter in async Apex
Callout first, then the DML update — correctly ordered since the callout completes before any DML is pending in that transaction
questions.explain: The callout happens first and completes before the DML update, satisfying the rule that a callout can't happen while DML is pending in the same transaction.

questions.q: What happens in this project's design after the retry attempt cap (3 attempts) is reached?
options: A durable Order_Sync_Failure__c record is created so the failure isn't silently lost
The original Order__c record is deleted
The Named Credential is automatically disabled
The job retries indefinitely with no cap
questions.explain: Once the attempt cap is reached, the job writes a durable failure record rather than retrying forever or failing silently, reusing the Lesson 6 retry pattern.

questions.q: Why does this lesson emphasize that the OrderSyncJob's update must be idempotent?
options: Because idempotency is required by the 100-callouts-per-transaction governor limit
Because the job can retry, and re-running it with the same order shouldn't cause a problem — a plain field overwrite is safe, unlike an operation that would double-count on retry
Because Queueable Apex automatically runs every job twice
Because idempotency is only relevant to SOAP callouts
questions.explain: Since the job may retry, its side effects need to be safe to repeat — overwriting a status field is safe, but an operation like incrementing a counter would not be.

questions.q: What approach does this lesson suggest for simulating the external order system without a real third-party dependency?
options: Use a Platform Event instead of a callout
Skip testing the callout entirely
Point the Named Credential at a request-echoing test service, or write a throwaway Apex REST service in the same org returning a fake status
Hard-code the fulfillment status directly in the trigger
questions.explain: A free echoing test service or a self-built Apex REST endpoint in the same org lets the full round trip be tested without any real external dependency.
